description: Formal mapping of core systems research questions to baseline comparisons, experimental implementations, evaluation metrics, and verified empirical evidence.

experiments.research_question: Can a new service be added without changing existing service implementations?
experiments.hypothesis: H1: The MCP-based architecture can integrate an additional specialized service while limiting changes to existing service implementations and preserving existing service interfaces.
experiments.verified_result: 0 existing service files modified, 0 existing service LOC modified, 11/11 schema fields matched, 100% workflow completion rate across 5 retail categories.

experiments.research_question: Can a service be replaced while preserving the interface and downstream decision consumption?
experiments.hypothesis: A specialized service can be replaced with an alternative algorithm without modifying upstream/downstream services or degrading interface contracts.
experiments.retailops_implementation: Replacement Forecasting MCP Server (60-day moving average variant in servers/forecasting-replacement/server.py)
experiments.verified_result: 0 existing sibling services modified, identical getForecast schema preserved, 100% downstream consumption by replenishment and pricing nodes.

experiments.research_question: What is the runtime cost and process-lifecycle overhead of process-based MCP execution?
experiments.hypothesis: Process-per-call MCP execution introduces measurable process-lifecycle overhead compared to direct in-process function invocation.
experiments.retailops_implementation: MCP process-per-call orchestrator (client/orchestrator.py launching servers per node)
experiments.verified_result: Direct in-process execution achieves ~1-5ms mean latency; MCP process-per-call requires ~1.5-2.0s per service spawn on Windows, demonstrating that process-spawn dominates runtime.

experiments.research_question: What is the effect of persistent MCP sessions on workflow execution latency?
experiments.hypothesis: Reusing long-lived MCP server processes amortizes process spawn overhead and isolates pure IPC protocol communication time.
experiments.retailops_implementation: Persistent MCP session pool (client/persistent_client.py, Condition C)
experiments.verified_result: Persistent session reuse eliminates repeated OS subprocess spawn, reducing subsequent execution latency by >85% compared to process-per-call.

experiments.research_question: How does the workflow behave under service failure, and does it guarantee downstream protection and OS-level cleanup?
experiments.hypothesis: An explicit state-based orchestration layer with MCP boundaries detects service failures, preserves partial results, prevents downstream cascades, and ensures complete OS process termination.
experiments.baseline: Expected failure behavior across 6 formal fault scenarios (A through F)
experiments.retailops_implementation: LangGraph node-level state guards, failed_enrichment downstream protection, and psutil-verified process exit
experiments.verified_result: 100% failure detection across all 6 scenarios, 100% downstream protection prevented calls after upstream failures, 0 zombie processes confirmed via psutil.

experiments.research_question: How does RetailOps compare architecturally with published state-of-the-art retail agent frameworks such as Flowr?
experiments.hypothesis: RetailOps and Flowr share overlapping goals in decomposing retail operations via MCP, but differ fundamentally in orchestration strategy, governance philosophy, evaluation focus, and public reproducibility.
experiments.baseline: Documented literature evidence from Flowr (Bandara et al., 2026, arXiv:2604.05987)
experiments.retailops_implementation: RetailOps verified implementation and empirical experiment artifacts
experiments.verified_result: 17 architectural dimensions analyzed; evidence strictly classified into literature, implementation, and experiment tiers; preliminary evidence documented with no unsupported superiority claims.
